entries.512aa3b6d94c5e7497e06ff49c420e9b0994565e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv130"/><title type="x-s4">Completed by <hi type="small-caps">John Reynolds, of Shrewsbury</hi> .</title> <div sID="gen33824" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">Christian</hi> communion is exerted and cherished by letter. Christians are to be commended in the practical proof of their professed subjection to the gospel of Christ. The animating and countenancing of generous and public-spirited persons is doing good to many—to this end the apostle sends this encouraging epistle to his friend Gaius, in which also he complains of the quite opposite spirit and practice of a certain minister, and confirms the good report concerning another more worthy to be imitated. <div eID="gen33824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33825" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33826" type="x-p"/> In this epistle the apostle congratulates Gaius upon the prosperity of his soul (<reference osisRef="3John.1.1-3John.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), upon the fame he had among good Christians (<reference osisRef="3John.1.3-3John.1.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>), and upon his charity and hospitality to the servants of Christ, <reference osisRef="3John.1.5-3John.1.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. He complains of contemptuous treatment by an ambitious Diotrephes, (<reference osisRef="3John.1.9-3John.1.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>), recommends Demetrius, (<reference osisRef="3John.1.12">ver. 12</reference>), and expresses his hope of visiting Gaius shortly, <reference osisRef="3John.1.13-3John.1.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv130"/> <div eID="gen33826" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33825" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Salutation and Prayer. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 90.)</title> <div sID="gen33827" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The elder unto the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth. <hi type="super">2</hi> Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth. <div eID="gen33827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33828" type="x-p"/> Here we see, I. The sacred penman who writes and sends the letter; not here indeed notified by his name, but a more general character: <hi type="italic">The elder,</hi> he that is so by years and by office; honour and deference are due to both. Some have questioned whether this were John the apostle or no; but his style and spirit seem to shine in the epistle. Those that are beloved of Christ will love the brethren for his sake. Gaius could not question from whom the letter came. The apostle might have assumed many more illustrious characters, but it becomes not Christ's ministers to affect swelling pompous titles. He almost levels himself with the more ordinary pastors of the church, while he styles himself the elder. Or, possibly, most of the extraordinary ministers, the apostles, were now dead, and this holy survivor would countenance the continued standing ministry, by assuming the more common title—the elder. <hi type="italic">The elders I exhort, who am also an elder,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1">1 Pet. v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen33828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33829" type="x-p"/> II. The person saluted and honoured by the letter. The former is directed to an elect lady, this to a choice gentleman; such are worthy of esteem and value. He is notified, 1. By his name,—<hi type="italic">Gaius.</hi> We read of several of that name, particularly of one whom the apostle Paul baptized at Corinth, who possibly might be also the apostle's host and kind entertainer there (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.23">Rom. xvi. 23</reference>); if this be not he, it is his brother in name, estate, and disposition. Then, 2. By the kind expressions of the apostle to him: <hi type="italic">The well-beloved,</hi> and <hi type="italic">whom I love in the truth.</hi> Love expressed is wont to kindle love. Here seems to be either the sincerity of the apostle's love or the religion of it. The sincerity of it: <hi type="italic">Whom I love in the truth,</hi> for the truth's sake, as abiding and walking in the truth as it is in Jesus. To love our friends for the truth's sake is true love, religious gospel love. <div eID="gen33829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33830" type="x-p"/> III. The salutation or greeting, containing a prayer, introduced by an affectionate compellation—<hi type="italic">Beloved,</hi> thou beloved one in Christ. The minister who would gain love must show it himself. Here is, 1. The apostle's good opinion of his friend, that his <hi type="italic">soul prospered.</hi> There is such a thing as soul-prosperity—the greatest blessing on this side heaven. This supposes regeneration, and an inward fund of spiritual life; this stock is increasing, and, while spiritual treasures are advancing, the soul is in a fair way to the kingdom of glory. 2. His good wish for his friend that his body may <hi type="italic">prosper and be in health</hi> as well as his soul. Grace and health are two rich companions; grace will improve health, health will employ grace. It frequently falls out that a rich soul is lodged in a crazy body; grace must be exercised in submission to such a dispensation; but we may well wish and pray that those who have prosperous souls may have healthful bodies too; their grace will shine in a larger sphere of activity.
entries.427b5881a90ef94caaefc9372f349ddcec6862b2: <div eID="gen33830" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Character of Gaius. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 90.)</title> <div sID="gen33831" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> For I rejoiced greatly, when the brethren came and testified of the truth that is in thee, even as thou walkest in the truth. <hi type="super">4</hi> I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth. <hi type="super">5</hi> Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers; <hi type="super">6</hi> Which have borne witness of thy charity before the church: whom if thou bring forward on their journey after a godly sort, thou shalt do well: <hi type="super">7</hi> Because that for his name's sake they went forth, taking nothing of the Gentiles. <hi type="super">8</hi> We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth. <div eID="gen33831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33832" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen33832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33833" type="x-p"/> I. The good report that the apostle had received concerning this friend of his: <hi type="italic">The brethren came and testified of the truth that is in thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="3John.1.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">who have borne witness of thy charity before the church,</hi> <reference osisRef="3John.1.6">v. 6</reference>. Here we may see, 1. The testimony or thing testified concerning Gaius—the truth that was in him, the reality of his faith, the sincerity of his religion, and his devotedness to God; and this evinced by his charity, which includes his love to the brethren, kindness to the poor, hospitality to Christian strangers, and readiness to accommodate them for the service of the gospel. Faith should work by love; it gives a lustre in and by the offices of love, and induces others to commend its integrity. 2. The witnesses-brethren that came from Gaius testified and bore witness. A good report is due from those who have received good; though a good name is but a small reward for costly service, yet it is <hi type="italic">better than precious ointment,</hi> and will not be refused by the ingenuous and religious. 3. The auditory or judicatory before which the report and testimony were given—<hi type="italic">before the church.</hi> This seems to be the church at which the apostle now resided. What church this was we are not sure; what occasion they had thus to testify his faith and love before the church we cannot tell; possibly out of the fulness of the heart the mouth spoke; they could not but testify what they found and felt; possibly they would engage the church's prayer for the continued life and usefulness of such a patron, that he might <hi type="italic">prosper and be in health as his soul prospered.</hi> <div eID="gen33833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33834" type="x-p"/> II. The report the apostle himself gives of him, introduced by an endearing appellation again: <hi type="italic">Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers,</hi> <reference osisRef="3John.1.5">v. 5</reference>. 1. He was hospitable, good to the brethren, even to strangers; it was enough to recommend them to Gaius's house that they belonged to Christ. Or he was good to <hi type="italic">the brethren</hi> of the same church with himself, and to those who came from far; all who were of the household of faith were welcome to him. 2. He seems to have been of a catholic spirit; he could overlook the petty differences among serious Christians, and be communicative to all who bore the image and did the work of Christ. And, 3. He was conscientious in what he did: "<hi type="italic">Thou doest faithfully</hi> (thou makest faithful work of) <hi type="italic">whatsoever thou doest;</hi> thou doest it as a faithful servant, and from the Lord Christ mayest thou expect the reward of the inheritance." Such faithful souls can hear their own praises without being puffed up; the commendation of what is good in us is designed, not for our pride, but for our encouragement to continue therein, and should be accordingly improved. <div eID="gen33834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33835" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle's joy therein, in the good report itself, and the good ground of it: <hi type="italic">I rejoiced greatly when the brethren came and testified,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="3John.1.3">v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in the truth,</hi> in the prescripts of the Christian religion. The best evidence of our having the truth is our <hi type="italic">walking in the truth.</hi> Good men will greatly rejoice in the soul-prosperity of others; and they are glad to hear of the grace and goodness of others. <hi type="italic">They glorified God in me.</hi> Love envieth not, but rejoiceth in the good name of other folks. As it is joy to good parents, it will be joy to good ministers, to see their children evidence their sincerity in religion, and adorn their profession. <div eID="gen33835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33836" type="x-p"/> IV. The direction the apostle gives his friend concerning further treatment of the brethren that were with him: <hi type="italic">Whom if thou bring forward on their journey, after a godly sort, thou shalt do well.</hi> It seems to have been customary in those days of love to attend travelling ministers and Christians, at least some part of their road, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.6">1 Cor. xvi. 6</reference>. It is a kindness to a stranger to be guided in his way, and a pleasure to travellers to meet with suitable company: this is a work that may be done <hi type="italic">after a godly sort,</hi> in a manner worthy of God, or suitable to the deference and relation we bear to God. Christians should consider not only what they must do, but what they may do, what they may most honourably and laudably do: <hi type="italic">the liberal mind deviseth liberal</hi> generous <hi type="italic">things.</hi> Christians should do even the common actions of life and of good-will after a godly sort, as serving God therein, and designing his glory. <div eID="gen33836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33837" type="x-p"/> V. The reasons of this directed conduct; these are two:—1. <hi type="italic">Because that for his name's sake these brethren went forth, taking nothing of the Gentiles.</hi> It appears thus that these were ministerial brethren, that they went forth to preach the gospel and propagate Christianity; possibly they might be sent out by this apostle himself: they went forth to convert the Gentiles; this was excellent service: they went forth for God and his name's sake; this is the minister's highest end, and should be his principal spring and motive, to gather and to build up a people for his name: they went forth also to carry a free gospel about with them, to publish it without charge wherever they came: <hi type="italic">Taking nothing of the Gentiles.</hi> These were worthy of double honour. There are those who are not called to preach the gospel themselves who may yet contribute to the progress of it. The gospel should be made without charge to those to whom it is first preached. Those who know it not cannot be expected to value it; churches and Christian patriots ought to concur to support the propagation of holy religion in the pagan countries; public spirits should concur according to their several capacities; those who are freely communicative of Christ's gospel should be assisted by those who are communicative of their purses. 2. <hi type="italic">We ought therefore to receive such, that we may be fellow-helpers to the truth,</hi> to true religion. The institution of Christ is the true religion; it has been attested by God. Those that are true in it and true to it will earnestly desire, and pray for, and contribute to, its propagation in the world. In many ways may the truth be befriended and assisted; those who cannot themselves proclaim it may yet receive, accompany, help, and countenance those who do.
entries.0224c5047e5f4e1f01db9f0b81fbe57f3037aeea: <div eID="gen33837" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Character of Diotrephes. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 90.)</title> <div sID="gen33838" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not. <hi type="super">10</hi> Wherefore, if I come, I will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against us with malicious words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth <hi type="italic">them</hi> out of the church. <hi type="super">11</hi> Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God. <div eID="gen33838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33839" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a very different example and character, an officer, a minister in the church, less generous, catholic, and communicative than the private Christians. Ministers may sometimes be out-shone, out-done. In reference to this minister, we see, <div eID="gen33839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33840" type="x-p"/> 1. His name—a Gentile name: <hi type="italic">Diotrephes,</hi> attended with an unchristian spirit. <div eID="gen33840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33841" type="x-p"/> 2. His temper and spirit—full of pride and ambition: <hi type="italic">He loves to have the pre-eminence.</hi> This ferment sprang and wrought betimes. It is an ill unbeseeming character of Christ's ministers to love pre-eminence, to affect presidency in the church of God. <div eID="gen33841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33842" type="x-p"/> 3. His contempt of the apostle's authority, and letter, and friends. (1.) Of his authority: <hi type="italic">The deeds which he doeth</hi> contrary to our appointment, <hi type="italic">prating against us with malicious words.</hi> Strange that the contempt should run so high! But ambition will breed malice against those who oppose it. Malice and ill-will in the heart will be apt to vent themselves by the lips. The heart and mouth are both to be watched. (2.) Of his letter: "<hi type="italic">I wrote to the church</hi> (<reference osisRef="3John.1.9">v. 9</reference>), namely, in recommendation of such and such brethren. <hi type="italic">But Diotrephes receiveth us not,</hi> admits not our letter and testimony therein." This seems to be the church of which Gaius was a member. A gospel church seems to be such a society as to which a letter may be written and communicated. Gospel churches may well expect and be allowed credentials with the strangers who desire to be admitted among them. The apostle seems to write by and with these brethren. To an ambitious aspiring spirit apostolical authority or epistle signifies but little. (3.) Of his friends, the brethren he recommended: <hi type="italic">Neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth those that would, and casteth them out of the church,</hi> <reference osisRef="3John.1.10">v. 10</reference>. There might be some differences or different customs between the Jewish and Gentile Christians. Pastors should seriously consider what differences are tolerable. The pastor is not at absolute liberty, nor lord over God's heritage. It is bad to do no good ourselves; but it is worse to hinder those who would. Church-power and church-censures are often abused. Many are cast out of the church who should be received there with satisfaction and welcome. But woe to those who cast out the brethren whom the Lord Christ will take into his own communion and kingdom! <div eID="gen33842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33843" type="x-p"/> 4. The apostle's menace of this proud domineerer: <hi type="italic">Wherefore, if I come, I will remember his deeds which he doeth</hi> (<reference osisRef="3John.1.10">v. 10</reference>), will remember to censure them. This seems to intimate apostolical authority. But the apostle seems not to hold an episcopal court, to which Diotrephes must be summoned; but he will come to take cognizance of this affair in the church to which it belongs. Acts of ecclesiastical domination and tyranny ought to be animadverted upon. May it be better agreed to whom that power belongs! <div eID="gen33843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33844" type="x-p"/> II. Here is counsel upon that different character, dissuasion from copying such a pattern, and indeed any evil at all: <hi type="italic">Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good,</hi> <reference osisRef="3John.1.11">v. 11</reference>. Imitate not such unchristian pernicious evil; but pursue the contrary good, in wisdom, purity, peace, and love. Caution and counsel are not needless to those who are good already. Those cautions and counsels are most likely to be accepted that are seasoned with love. <hi type="italic">Beloved, follow not that which is evil.</hi> To this caution and counsel a reason is respectively subjoined. 1. To the counsel: <hi type="italic">Follow that which is good;</hi> for <hi type="italic">he that doeth good</hi> (naturally and genuinely doeth good, as delighting therein) <hi type="italic">is of God,</hi> is born of God. The practice of goodness is the evidence of our filial happy relation to God. 2. To the caution: <hi type="italic">Follow not that which is evil,</hi> for <hi type="italic">he that doeth evil</hi> (with bent of mind pursues it) <hi type="italic">hath not seen God,</hi> is not duly sensible of his holy nature and will. Evil-workers vainly pretend or boast an acquaintance with God.
entries.a65072cb77928227ea613c88759a1384919414f7: <div eID="gen33844" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Character of Demetrius; Conclusion and Salutation. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 90.)</title> <div sID="gen33845" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Demetrius hath good report of all <hi type="italic">men,</hi> and of the truth itself: yea, and we <hi type="italic">also</hi> bear record; and ye know that our record is true. <hi type="super">13</hi> I had many things to write, but I will not with ink and pen write unto thee: <hi type="super">14</hi> But I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face. Peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> to thee. <hi type="italic">Our</hi> friends salute thee. Greet the friends by name. <div eID="gen33845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33846" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. The character of another person, one <hi type="italic">Demetrius,</hi> not much known otherwise. But here his name will live. A name in the gospel, a fame in the churches, is better than that of sons and daughters. His character was his commendation. His commendation was, 1. General: <hi type="italic">Demetrius has a good report of all men.</hi> Few are well spoken of by all; and sometimes it is ill to be so. But universal integrity and goodness are the way to (and sometimes obtain) universal applause. 2. Deserved and well founded: <hi type="italic">And of the truth itself,</hi> <reference osisRef="3John.1.12">v. 12</reference>. Some have a good report, but not of the truth itself. Happy are those whose spirit and conduct commend them before God and men. 3. Confirmed by the apostle's and his friends' testimony: <hi type="italic">Yea, and we also bear record;</hi> and that with an appeal to Gaius's own knowledge: <hi type="italic">And you</hi> (you and your friends) <hi type="italic">know that our record is true.</hi> Probably this Demetrius was known to the church where the apostle now resided, and to that where Gaius was. It is good to be well known, or known for good. We must be ready to bear our testimony to those who are good: it is well for those who are commended when those who commend them can appeal to the consciences of those who know them most. <div eID="gen33846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33847" type="x-p"/> II. The conclusion of the epistle, in which we may observe, 1. The referring of some things to personal interview: <hi type="italic">I have many things to write, but I will not with ink and pen, but I trust I shall shortly see thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="3John.1.13-3John.1.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Many things may be more proper for immediate communication than for letter. A little personal conference may spare the time, trouble, and charge, of many letters; and good Christians may well be glad to see one another. 2. The benediction: <hi type="italic">Peace be to you;</hi> all felicity attend you. Those that are good and happy themselves wish others so too. 3. The public salutation sent to Gaius: <hi type="italic">Our friends salute thee.</hi> A friend to the propagation of religion deserves a common remembrance. And these pious persons show their friendship to religion as well as to Gaius. 4. The apostle's particular salutation of the Christians in Gaius's church or vicinity: <hi type="italic">Greet thy friends by name.</hi> I doubt they were not very many who must be so personally saluted. But we must learn humility as well as love. The lowest in the church of Christ should be greeted. And those may well salute and greet one another on earth who hope to live together in heaven. And the apostle who had lain in Christ's bosom lays Christ's friends in his heart.  <chapter eID="3John.1"/> <div eID="gen33847" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen33821" osisID="3John" type="book"/>

entries.b31d0db1e5a7ddc41679117e8bbadbe87a2d5ff7: <chapter n="1" osisID="3John.1" sID="3John.1"/> 3Jo 1-14. Address: Wish for Gaius' Prosperity: Joy at His Walking in the Truth. Hospitality to the Brethren and Strangers the Fruit of Love. Diotrephes' Opposition and Ambition. Praise of Demetrius. Conclusion.<div eID="gen41004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41005" type="x-p"/>
entries.213b2f90d3c3e0c7b6f4bbe5d0fd95e1562c598f: <hi type="bold">1. I--</hi>emphatical. I personally, for my part. On Gaius or Caius, see my Introduction before Second Epistle.<div eID="gen41005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love in the truth--</hi>(2Jo 1). "Beloved" is repeated often in this Epistle, indicating strong affection (<reference osisRef="3John.1.2">3Jo 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.11">5, 11</reference>). <div eID="gen41006" type="x-p"/>
entries.cbbfc6a24dca666a61af4db71bc46c93fa195f56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19010"/><div sID="gen41007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19010"/><hi type="bold">2. above all things--</hi>Greek, "concerning all things": so Alford: in all respects. But Wahl justifies English Version (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">1Pe 4:8</reference>). Of course, since his soul's prosperity is presupposed, "above all things" does not imply that John wishes Gaius' bodily health above that of his soul, but as the first object to be desired next after spiritual health. I know you are prospering in the concerns of your soul. I wish you similar prosperity in your body. Perhaps John had heard from the brethren (3Jo 3) that Gaius was in bad health, and was tried in other ways (3Jo 10), to which the wish, 3Jo 2, refers.<div eID="gen41007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prosper--</hi>in general.<div eID="gen41008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be in health--</hi>in particular. <div eID="gen41009" type="x-p"/>
entries.9797edf79179fab4f9b0a8e227b7633dcbcc7710: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19011"/><div sID="gen41010" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19011"/><hi type="bold">3. testified of the truth that is in thee--</hi>Greek, "of" (or 'to') thy truth": thy share of that truth in which thou walkest [Alford].<div eID="gen41010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even as thou--</hi>in contrast to Diotrephes (3Jo 9). <div eID="gen41011" type="x-p"/>
entries.74cce75b7dea7b7b82134bb1d34dcd3e74201312: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19012"/><div sID="gen41012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19012"/><hi type="bold">4. my children--</hi>members of the Church: confirming the view that the "elect lady" is a Church. <div eID="gen41012" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9a402879a849aa933ca7152bd468701b5854d7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19013"/><div sID="gen41013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19013"/><hi type="bold">5. faithfully--</hi>an act becoming a faithful man.<div eID="gen41013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whatsoever thou doest--</hi>a distinct Greek word from the former "doest": translate, "workest": whatsoever work, or labor of love, thou dost perform. So <reference osisRef="Matt.26.10">Mt 26:10</reference>, "She hath wrought a good work upon me."<div eID="gen41014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and to strangers--</hi>The oldest manuscripts, "and that (that is, and those brethren) strangers." The fact of the brethren whom thou didst entertain being "strangers," enhances the love manifested in the act. <div eID="gen41015" type="x-p"/>
entries.e382b0fd76451efcd7a419c3ce0bf6ec02f1ad11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19014"/><div sID="gen41016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19014"/><hi type="bold">6. borne witness of thy charity before the church--</hi>to stimulate others by the good example. The brethren so entertained by Gaius were missionary evangelists (3Jo 7); and, probably, in the course of narrating their missionary labors for the edification of the Church where John then was, incidentally mentioned the loving hospitality shown them by Gaius.<div eID="gen41016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring forward on their journey--</hi>"If thou (continue to) forward on their journey" by giving them provisions for the way.<div eID="gen41017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after a godly sort--</hi>Greek, "in a manner worthy of God," whose ambassadors they are, and whose servant thou art. He who honors God's missionary servants (3Jo 7), honors God. <div eID="gen41018" type="x-p"/>
entries.40586f141191d370a3d32cf699bced6af65f659f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19015"/><div sID="gen41019" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19015"/><hi type="bold">7. his name's sake--</hi>Christ's.<div eID="gen41019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went forth--</hi>as missionaries.<div eID="gen41020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taking nothing--</hi>refusing to receive aught by way of pay, or maintenance, though justly entitled to it, as Paul at Corinth and at Thessalonica.<div eID="gen41021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gentiles--</hi>the Christians just gathered out by their labors from among the heathen. As Gaius himself was a Gentile convert, "the Gentiles" here must mean the converts just made from the heathen, the Gentiles to whom they had gone forth. It would have been inexpedient to have taken aught (the Greek "meden" implies, not that they got nothing, though they had desired it, but that it was of their own choice they took nothing) from the infant churches among the heathen: the case was different in receiving hospitality from Gaius. <div eID="gen41022" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e549b3af11593c502f7320ddc0f1b7da0ee3de8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19016"/><div sID="gen41023" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19016"/><hi type="bold">8. We--</hi>in contradistinction to "the Gentiles" or "heathen" referred to, 3Jo 7.<div eID="gen41023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>as they take nothing from the Gentiles or heathen.<div eID="gen41024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receive--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "take up." As they "take" nothing from the Gentiles, we ought to take them up so as to support them.<div eID="gen41025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fellow helpers--</hi>with them.<div eID="gen41026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the truth--</hi>that is, to promote the truth. <div eID="gen41027" type="x-p"/>
entries.423093cd0ef6185ec99ba121a71b01e48a21effd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19017"/><div sID="gen41028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19017"/><hi type="bold">9. I wrote--</hi>The oldest manuscripts add "something": a communication, probably, on the subject of receiving the brethren with brotherly love (3Jo 8, 10). That Epistle was not designed by the Spirit for the universal Church, or else it would have been preserved.<div eID="gen41028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the church--</hi>of which Gaius is a member.<div eID="gen41029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loveth ... pre-eminence--</hi>through ambition. Evidently occupying a high place in the Church where Gaius was (3Jo 10).<div eID="gen41030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among them--</hi>over the members of the Church.<div eID="gen41031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receiveth us not--</hi>virtually, namely, by not receiving with love the brethren whom we recommended to be received (3Jo 8, 10; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.10.40">Mt 10:40</reference>). <div eID="gen41032" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0684e3a1f4e8570b7e179c8d3b02d8c6be26942: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19018"/><div sID="gen41033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19018"/><hi type="bold">10. if I come--</hi>(3Jo 14).<div eID="gen41033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will remember--</hi>literally, "I will bring to mind" before all by stigmatizing and punishing.<div eID="gen41034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prating--</hi>with mere silly tattle.<div eID="gen41035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither doth he ... receive the brethren--</hi>with hospitality. "The brethren" are the missionaries on their journey.<div eID="gen41036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forbiddeth them that would--</hi>receive them.<div eID="gen41037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">casteth them--</hi>those that would receive the brethren, by excommunication from the Church, which his influence, as a leading man (3Jo 9) in it, enabled him to do. Neander thinks that the missionaries were Jews by birth, whence it is said in their praise they took nothing from THE Gentiles: in contrast to other Jewish missionaries who abused ministers' right of maintenance elsewhere, as Paul tells us, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.22">2Co 11:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.2">Php 3:2</reference>, 5, 19. Now in the Gentile churches there existed an ultra-Pauline party of anti-Jewish tendency, the forerunners of Marcion: Diotrephes possibly stood at the head of this party, which fact, as well as this domineering spirit, may account for his hostility to the missionaries, and to the apostle John, who had, by the power of love, tried to harmonize the various elements in the Asiatic churches. At a later period, Marcion, we know, attached himself to Paul alone, and paid no deference to the authority of John. <div eID="gen41038" type="x-p"/>
entries.14cf1b4d696e9af2a3d01704a44aa9c8fd6a59c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19019"/><div sID="gen41039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19019"/><hi type="bold">11. follow not that which is evil--</hi>as manifested in Diotrephes (3Jo 9, 10).<div eID="gen41039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but ... good--</hi>as manifested in Demetrius (3Jo 12).<div eID="gen41040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is of God--</hi>is born of God, who is good.<div eID="gen41041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath not seen God--</hi>spiritually, not literally. <div eID="gen41042" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c2cd5b1ada16cb5c268b2eeb12cd1f7c692825d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19020"/><div sID="gen41043" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19020"/><hi type="bold">12. of all men--</hi>who have had opportunity of knowing his character.<div eID="gen41043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the truth itself--</hi>The Gospel standard of truth bears witness to him that he walks conformably to it, in acts of real love, hospitality to the brethren (in contrast to Diotrephes), &c. Compare <reference osisRef="John.3.21">Joh 3:21</reference> "He that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest that they are wrought in God."<div eID="gen41044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we also--</hi>besides the testimony of "all men," and "of the truth itself."<div eID="gen41045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye know--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "thou knowest." <div eID="gen41046" type="x-p"/>
entries.81aab5fec4546dc86bd7e319fc40ab8583429d4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19021"/><div sID="gen41047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19021"/><hi type="bold">13. I will not--</hi>rather as Greek, "I wish not ... to write" more. <div eID="gen41047" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b2b2899fa1a35b010c492561e3fea34a74dede8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19022"/><div sID="gen41048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19022"/><hi type="bold">14. face to face--</hi>Greek, "mouth to mouth."<div eID="gen41048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Peace--</hi>peace inward of conscience, peace fraternal of friendship, peace supernal of glory [Lyra].<div eID="gen41049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">friends--</hi>a title seldom used in the New Testament, as it is absorbed in the higher titles of "brother, brethren." Still Christ recognizes the relation of friend also, based on the highest grounds, obedience to Him from love, and entailing the highest privileges, admission to the intimacy of the holy and glorious God, and sympathizing Saviour; so Christians have "friends" in Christ. Here in a friendly letter, mention of "friends" appropriately occurs.<div eID="gen41050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by name--</hi>not less than if their names were written [Bengel]. <chapter eID="3John.1"/><div eID="gen41051" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen41002" osisID="3John" type="book"/>

entries.3e5a0f98760631771edd9b2f9e6f2e1617e04ff0: <div eID="gen55392" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Third Epistle of John</title> <div sID="gen55393" type="x-p"/> This epistle being of nearly the same complexion with the former, and evidently written about the same time, and incontestably by the same person, it is not necessary to give it any particular preface; as the subject of the authenticity of all the three epistles has been treated already so much at large, not only in the introduction to them, but in the notes in general. <div eID="gen55393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55394" type="x-p"/> This and the preceding epistle are, by Dr. Lardner, supposed to have been written between a.d. 80 and 90. There are no notes of time in the epistles themselves to help us to fix any date, therefore all is conjecture concerning the time in which they were written: but to me it appears as likely that they were written before the destruction of Jerusalem as after; for it is scarcely to be supposed that so signal a display of the justice of God, and such a powerful argument in favor of Christianity and of the truth of Christ's predictions, could be passed unnoticed and unappealed to by any of the inspired persons who wrote after that event. However, where there is no positive evidence, conjecture is useless. <div eID="gen55394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55395" type="x-p"/> The apostle's address to Caius, and his good wishes for his prosperity in body and soul, <reference osisRef="3Jn.1.1">3Jn 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="3Jn.1.2">3Jn 1:2</reference>. He commends him for his steadiness in the truth, and his general hospitality, especially to the itinerant evangelists, <reference osisRef="3Jn.1.3-3Jn.1.8">3Jn 1:3-8</reference>. Speaks of the bad conduct of Diotrephes; his abuse of his power in the Church; and his slander of the apostles, <reference osisRef="3Jn.1.9">3Jn 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="3Jn.1.10">3Jn 1:10</reference>. Exhorts Caius to avoid his example, and to follow what is good, <reference osisRef="3Jn.1.11">3Jn 1:11</reference>. Commends Demetrius, <reference osisRef="3Jn.1.12">3Jn 1:12</reference>. Excuses himself from writing more fully, and proposes to pay him a visit shortly, <reference osisRef="3Jn.1.13">3Jn 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="3Jn.1.14">3Jn 1:14</reference>. <div eID="gen55395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55396" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen55396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55397" type="x-p"/> The elder - See on the first verse of the preceding epistle (<reference osisRef="2Jn.1.1">2Jn 1:1</reference> (note), and also the preface. <div eID="gen55397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55398" type="x-p"/> The well-beloved Gaius - Γαιος Gaius, is the Greek mode of writing the Roman name Caius; and thus it should be rendered in European languages. <div eID="gen55398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55399" type="x-p"/> Several persons of the name of Caius occur in the New Testament. <div eID="gen55399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55400" type="x-p"/> 1. In the Epistle to the Romans, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.23">Rom 16:23</reference>, St. Paul mentions a Caius who lived at Corinth, whom he calls his host, and the host of the whole Church. <div eID="gen55400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55401" type="x-p"/> 2. In <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">1Cor 1:14</reference>, St. Paul mentions a Caius who lived at Corinth, whom he had baptized; but this is probably the same with the above. <div eID="gen55401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55402" type="x-p"/> 3. In <reference osisRef="Act.19.29">Act 19:29</reference>, mention is made of a Caius who was a native of Macedonia, who accompanied St. Paul, and spent some time with him at Ephesus. This is probably a different person from the preceding; for the description given of the Caius who lived at Corinth, and was the host of the whole Church there, does not accord with the description of the Macedonian Caius, who, in the very same year, traveled with St. Paul, and was with him at Ephesus. <div eID="gen55402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55403" type="x-p"/> 4. In <reference osisRef="Act.20.4">Act 20:4</reference>, we meet a Caius of Derbe, who was likewise a fellow traveler of St. Paul. This person cannot be the Corinthian Caius, for the host of the Church at Corinth would hardly leave that city to travel into Asia: and he is clearly distinguishable from the Macedonian Caius by the epithet Δερβαιος, of Derbe. <div eID="gen55403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55404" type="x-p"/> 5. And lastly, there is the Caius who is mentioned here, and who is thought by some critics to be different from all the above; for, in writing to him, St. John ranks him among his children, which seems, according to them, to intimate that he was converted by this apostle. <div eID="gen55404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55405" type="x-p"/> Now, whether this Caius was one of the persons just mentioned, or whether he was different from them all, is difficult to determine; because Caius was a very common name. Yet if we may judge from the similarity of character, it is not improbable that he was the Caius who lived at Corinth, and who is styled by St. Paul the host of the whole Church; for hospitality to his Christian brethren was the leading feature in the character of this Caius to whom St. John wrote, and it is on this very account that he is commended by the apostle. Besides, St. John's friend lived in a place where this apostle had in Diotrephes a very ambitious and tyrannical adversary; and that there were men of this description at Corinth is evident enough from the two epistles to the Corinthians, though St. Paul has not mentioned their names. See Michaelis. <div eID="gen55405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55406" type="x-p"/> The probability of this Caius being the same with the Corinthian Caius has suggested the thought that this epistle was sent to Corinth; and consequently that the second epistle was sent to some place in the neighborhood of that city. But I think the distance between Ephesus, where St. John resided, and Corinth, was too considerable for such an aged man as St. John is represented to be to travel, whether by land or water. If he went by land, he must traverse a great part of Asia, go through Thrace, Macedonia, Thessaly, and down through Greece, to the Morea, a most tedious and difficult journey. If he went by water, he must cross the Aegean Sea, and navigate among the Cyclades Islands, which was always a dangerous voyage. Now as the apostle promises, both in the second and in this epistle, to see the persons shortly to whom he wrote, I take it for granted that they could not have lived at Corinth, or anywhere in the vicinity of that city. That St. John took such a voyage Michaelis thinks probable; "for since Corinth lay almost opposite to Ephesus, and St. John, from his former occupation, before he became an apostle, was accustomed to the sea, it is not improbable that the journey or voyage which he proposed to make was from Ephesus to Corinth." <div eID="gen55406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55407" type="x-p"/> In answer to this I would just observe, <div eID="gen55407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55408" type="x-p"/> 1. That the voyage was too long and dangerous for a man at John's advanced age to think of taking. <div eID="gen55408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55409" type="x-p"/> 2. That John had never been accustomed to any such sea as the Aegean, for the sea of Galilee, or sea of Tiberias, on which, as a fisherman, he got his bread, was only an inconsiderable fresh water lake; and his acquaintance with it could give him very few advantages for the navigation of the Aegean Sea, and the danger of coasting the numerous islands dispersed through it.
entries.7b18a49250e27981f8fe17eb72b00ffcb5c484ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen55409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55410" type="x-p"/> I wish above all things - Περι παντων ευχομαι· Above all things I pray that thou mayest prosper, and be in health, και ὑγιαινειν· to which one MS. adds εν αληθεια, which gives it a different meaning, viz., that thou mayest be sound in the truth. The prayer of St. John for Caius includes three particulars: <div eID="gen55410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55411" type="x-p"/> 1. Health of body; <div eID="gen55411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55412" type="x-p"/> 2. Health of soul; and <div eID="gen55412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55413" type="x-p"/> 3. Prosperity in secular affairs. That thou mayest Prosper and be in Health, as thy Soul Prospereth. These three things, so necessary to the comfort of life, every Christian may in a certain measure expect, and for them every Christian is authorized to pray; and we should have more of all three if we devoutly prayed for them. <div eID="gen55413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55414" type="x-p"/> It appears from the last clause that the soul of Caius was in a very prosperous state.
entries.2bc25f51805ef771bf30718bb7af866ecb2edf98: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen55414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55415" type="x-p"/> When the brethren came - Probably the same of whom he speaks in the fifth (<reference osisRef="3Jn.1.5">3Jn 1:5</reference>) and following verses, and who appear to have been itinerant evangelists. <div eID="gen55415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55416" type="x-p"/> The truth that is in thee - The soundness of thy faith and the depth of thy religion.
entries.8f27955f9f5b1b1b5e9334e5945518cac132f6ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen55416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55417" type="x-p"/> To hear that my children - From this it has been inferred that Caius was one of St. John's converts, and consequently not the Corinthian Caius, who was converted, most probably, by St. Paul. But the apostle might use the term children here as implying those who were immediately under his pastoral care, and, being an old man, he had a right to use such terms in addressing his juniors both in age and grace; and there is much both of propriety and dignity in the appellation coming from such a person.
entries.d70d51e833631f432bc834569d2c5dd0fdd2dfdb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen55417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55418" type="x-p"/> Thou doest faithfully - Πιστον ποιεις. Kypke thinks that πιστον is put here for πιστιν, and that the phrase signifies to keep or preserve the faith, or to be bound by the faith, or to keep one's engagements. Thou hast acted as the faith - the Christian religion, required thee to act, in all that thou hast done, both to the brethren at home, and to the strangers - the itinerant evangelists, who, in the course of their travels, have called at thy house. There is not a word here about the pilgrims and penitential journeys which the papists contrive to bring out of this text.
entries.3db129d9b2dc710c02469095eddca26d95de8288: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen55418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55419" type="x-p"/> Which have borne witness of thy charity - Of thy love and benevolence. <div eID="gen55419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55420" type="x-p"/> Before the Church - The believers at Ephesus; for to this Church the apostle seems to refer. <div eID="gen55420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55421" type="x-p"/> Whom if thou bring forward - If thou continue to assist such, as thou hast done, thou shalt do well. <div eID="gen55421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55422" type="x-p"/> The brethren of whom St. John speaks might have been apostles; the strangers, assistants to these apostles, as John Mark was to Barnabas. Both were itinerant evangelists. <div eID="gen55422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55423" type="x-p"/> After a godly sort - Αξιως του Θεου· Worthy of God; and in such a way as he can approve. Let all Churches, all congregations of Christians, from whom their ministers and preachers can claim nothing by law, and for whom the state makes no provision, lay this to heart; let them ask themselves, Do we deal with these in a manner worthy of God, and worthy of the profession we make? Do we suffer them to lack the bread that perisheth, while they minister to us with no sparing hand the bread of life? Let a certain class of religious people, who will find themselves out when they read this note, consider whether, when their preachers have ministered to them their certain or stated time, and are called to go and serve other Churches, they send them forth in a manner worthy of God, making a reasonable provision for the journey which they are obliged to take. In the itinerant ministry of the apostles it appears that each Church bore the expenses of the apostle to the next Church or district to which he was going to preach the word of life. So it should be still in the mission and itinerant ministry.
entries.044791e95bf3f04fea0fa5071179b98a8713e68a: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen55423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55424" type="x-p"/> For his name's sake they went forth - For the sake of preaching the Gospel of the grace of God, and making known Jesus to the heathen. <div eID="gen55424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55425" type="x-p"/> Taking nothing of the Gentiles - Receiving no emolument for their labor, but in every respect showing themselves to be truly disinterested. Sometimes, and on some special occasions, this may be necessary; but the laborer is worthy of his hire is the maxim of the author of Christianity. And those congregations of Christians are ever found to prize the Gospel most, and profit most by it, who bear all expenses incident to it, and vice versa. <div eID="gen55425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55426" type="x-p"/> But some construe εξηλθον, they went out, with απο των εθνων, from the Gentiles, or rather by the Gentiles, and give the passage this sense: They went out, i.e., were driven out by the Gentiles, taking nothing with them, i.e., leaving all their property behind, so that they were in a state of great destitution. A curious reading here, εθνικων, heathenish men, for εθνων, Gentiles, which latter might imply those who were converted from among the Gentiles, while the sense of the other term seems to be restrained to those who were still unconverted, may seem to strengthen the above interpretation; and although the construction seems rather harsh, yet it is not, on the whole, unlikely. The reading above referred to is that of the most ancient and reputable MSS. That to be driven out or expelled is one scriptural meaning of the verb εξερχομαι, see <reference osisRef="Mat.8.32">Mat 8:32</reference> : And when they were come out, οἱ δε εξελθοντεσς, and when they were Driven Out. <reference osisRef="Mat.12.43">Mat 12:43</reference> : When the unclean spirit is gone out, εξελθη, is Driven Out. See <reference osisRef="Mar.5.13">Mar 5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.7.29">Mar 7:29</reference> : The devil is gone out of thy daughter, εξεληλυθε, is Expelled. <reference osisRef="Mar.9.29">Mar 9:29</reference> : This kind can come forth by nothing εν ουδενι δυναται εξελθειν, can be Driven Out by nothing, but by prayer and fasting. <reference osisRef="Luk.8.2">Luk 8:2</reference> : Mary Magdalene; out of whom went, αφ' ἡς δαιμονια ἑπτα εξεληλυθει, out of whom were Cast, seven demons. See also <reference osisRef="1Jn.2.19">1Jn 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Rev 3:12</reference>; and Schleusner, in voc. εξερχομαι.
entries.fbd47f761726af20bf3a66bccdecc13ba9c96ff3: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen55426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55427" type="x-p"/> We therefore ought to receive such - Those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, and have professed the truth at the hazard of their lives, and the loss of all their worldly substance. Instead of απολαμβανειν, to receive, the most ancient and reputable MSS. have ὑπολαμβανειν, to take up, undertake for, or kindly receive. <div eID="gen55427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55428" type="x-p"/> Fellow helpers to the truth - And thus encourage the persecuted, and contribute to the spread and maintenance of the Gospel.
entries.543b41684f6cc659b4601c4dd43f2006ee448291: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen55428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55429" type="x-p"/> I wrote unto the Church - The Church where Caius was; but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the pre-eminence, φιλοπρωτευων, who loves the presidency, or chief place in the Church. He was doubtless an officer in the Church, at least a deacon, probably a bishop; and, being one, he magnified himself in his office; he loved such eminence, and behaved himself haughtily in it. <div eID="gen55429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55430" type="x-p"/> Receiveth us not - Does not acknowledge the apostolical authority. As some MSS. supply αν after εγραψα, and several judicious critics believe it is implied, the translation will run thus: I would have written to the Church to receive these men kindly, but Diotrephes, who affects the presidency; and into whose hands, if I wrote to the Church, my letter must come, receiveth us not - would not acknowledge my authority to interfere with any of the matters of his Church; and therefore I have written unto thee, whose love to the brethren and general hospitality are well known, that thou wouldst receive those strangers and persecuted followers of our common Lord.
entries.0aab308ca331f3d1c9a8bddafe75777918c0608e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen55430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55431" type="x-p"/> If I come, I will remember - I will show him the authority which, as an apostle of Jesus Christ, I possess. <div eID="gen55431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55432" type="x-p"/> Prating against us - Diotrephes might have been a converted Jew, who was unwilling that the Gentiles should be received into the Church; or a Judaizing Christian, who wished to incorporate the law with the Gospel, and calumniated the apostles who taught otherwise. This haughty and unfeeling man would give no countenance to the converted Gentiles; so far from it, that he would not receive any of them himself, forbade others to do it, and excommunicated those who had been received into the Church by the apostles. This appears to be the meaning of neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the Church. He had the complete dog in the manger principle: he would neither do, nor let do; and when good was done that he did not approve, he endeavored to undo it.
entries.70190f07d5f0fa878cf2b3361bf591416ec4472f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen55432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55433" type="x-p"/> Follow not that which is evil - Μμ μιμου το κακον· Do not imitate that wicked man, i.e., the conduct of Diotrephes; be merciful, loving, and kind. For whatever profession any man may make, it will ever appear that he who doeth good is of God - he alone is the person who uses rightly the grace received from God, and he alone shall enjoy the Divine approbation; <div eID="gen55433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55434" type="x-p"/> While he that doeth evil - He who is unfeeling, unmerciful, unkind, hath not seen God - has no proper knowledge of that God whose Name is mercy, and whose Nature is love.
entries.70a75015febd76e52907adc53638c65d590aea06: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen55434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55435" type="x-p"/> Demetrius hath good report - Perhaps another member of the Church where Caius was; or he might have been one of those whom the apostle recommends to Caius; or, possibly, the bearer of this letter from John to Caius. He seems to have been an excellent person: all testified of his righteousness; the truth - Christianity, itself bore testimony to him; and the apostles themselves added theirs also.
